articles.title: Colombia Hopes to Secure US Tariff Suspension Deal by Year-End - ColombiaOne.com
articles.summary: Colombia Hopes to Secure US Tariff Suspension Deal by Year-End  ColombiaOne.com
articles.full_text:
The government of Colombian President De la Espriella is working to reach an agreement with the United States to eliminate additional tariffs imposed on some of the South American country’s exports before the end of 2026. Trade Minister Mauricio Gomez Amin said bilateral talks are progressing at a good pace and that negotiating teams from both countries continue to work toward resolving their trade differences.
The goal is to restore market access conditions in the United States for Colombian products affected by the tariff measures adopted by Washington. The United States is one of Colombia’s main trading partners and a key destination for sectors such as flowers, coffee, processed foods, and manufactured goods.
The outcome of the negotiations could therefore affect exporters’ competitiveness, investment, and employment in the country.
Colombia hopes to secure US tariff suspension deal by year-end
Gomez Amin emphasized that talks with U.S. authorities are progressing favorably and that the Colombian government is seeking to reach an understanding before the end of the year.
“Last week, I was in Washington with Ambassador Maria Consuelo Araujo for a candid dialogue. We are making good progress. Our negotiators are sitting at the table right now,” the trade minister said in remarks to the media.
The statement reflects the efforts the new Colombian administration has been making for more than two months to secure the elimination of the tariffs, an objective that has been discussed since De la Espriella won the election in June.
“We are reviewing, article by article, what is best for both countries. That is what we are working on. We are optimistic that we might be able to reach a final agreement in the coming weeks and sign it in December. I cannot guarantee it, but it could happen this year,” Gomez Amin said.
The minister also announced trade agreements with El Salvador and Japan. “Colombia is open to the world. This is about enabling Colombia to export and attract high-level foreign investment in the coming months,” he said.
Señor Presidente @ABDELAESPRIELLA, ¡aquí estamos desde Washington cumpliendo la tarea! 🇨🇴🇺🇸
Junto a nuestra embajadora María Consuelo Araújo, hemos adelantado importantes conversaciones con el representante comercial de Estados Unidos, Jamieson Greer, con un objetivo claro: abrir más mercados para nuestras empresas, atraer inversión y traducir esta relación en más crecimiento y empleo para los colombianos.
¡Un verdadero gana-gana entre Colombia y Estados Unidos, nuestro principal socio comercial!
Bajo su liderazgo y siguiendo sus instrucciones, avanzamos en una agenda comercial estratégica basada en la confianza, la reciprocidad y los beneficios mutuos.

From 10% to 12.5%: how tariffs have changed
Negotiations with the United States are taking place amid successive changes in U.S. trade policy. On April 2, 2025, President Donald Trump announced a 10% baseline tariff on most imports from various countries, including Colombia. The measure took effect on April 5 of that year, ushering in a period of uncertainty for Colombian exporters.
Washington subsequently exempted certain Colombian products from the baseline tariff. These included coffee, bananas, avocados, cocoa, Tahiti limes, and goldenberries, according to trade decisions announced in 2025. These exemptions allowed some agricultural products to retain access to the U.S. market without the additional surcharge.
However, the situation changed again in July 2026. The U.S. government announced an additional 12.5% tariff on Colombia and other economies under investigation for failing to adopt or effectively enforce measures prohibiting imports of goods produced using forced labor.
The new tariff took effect on July 24 and applies to most Colombian imports that are not explicitly exempt. The measure provides exemptions for certain product categories, including raw materials whose availability could be affected by the tariffs and goods subject to other specific duties.
Therefore, the 12.5% tariff does not apply indiscriminately to all Colombian exports; the applicable treatment depends on each product’s classification and specific conditions.
A strategic trade relationship for both countries
The importance of resolving this dispute extends beyond the percentage charged on goods entering the United States. The U.S. market is an essential source of revenue for numerous Colombian companies and for industries that depend on international demand, including flower production, agribusiness, and manufacturing.
In 2024, Colombian exports to the United States reached $14.336 billion, equivalent to 28.9% of the country’s total exports, according to figures released by Colombia’s Ministry of Trade.
An agreement that reduces or eliminates the additional tariffs could improve the competitiveness of Colombian products relative to those from other countries, ease exporters’ costs, and support the continuity of bilateral business. For companies, it would also provide greater predictability when setting prices, negotiating contracts, and planning investments.
The De la Espriella government is betting on negotiations to achieve that outcome before the end of the year. So far, however, despite positive statements and expressions of goodwill from both sides, no agreement has materialized amid the tariff war waged by the Trump administration since last year.

articles.title: China's zero-tariff policy for Africa to benefit business, challenge US influence - thenational.co.za
articles.summary: China's zero-tariff policy for Africa to benefit business, challenge US influence  thenational.co.za
articles.full_text:
China's zero-tariff treatment for African countries is likely to benefit nations on the continent and is also a strategic move to counter the influence of the United States.
This was the view of Professor André Duvenhage, an International Relations expert from North West University, who said the zero-tariff move attempts to counter US influence in Africa and to rival the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) agreement, especially between South Africa and the United States.
Recently, the US extended AGOA to the end of 2028, bringing relief and more certainty for South African exporters who rely on duty-free access to the American market.
While highlighting that the AGOA agreement is critical for South Africa as an export market and for the car industry, Duvenhage said China's zero-tariff, announced by President Xi Jinping on 1 May 2026, will benefit some African countries.
”I believe that this (zero-tariff) can benefit some African countries without a doubt, especially when it comes to exporting strategic minerals. Otherwise, I think China would also like to see a market for its industrial products, because although China had a long and strong reputation for economic growth, they are currently facing economic challenges,” he said.
He added China's move is particularly significant amid growing global polarisation.
“It's part of the bigger context of power politics in the world, playing out on the terrain of the economy, finances, exports and imports. We know about all the blockades that are going on, American tariffs and so on. This is all part of a bigger political strategy,” he said.
Duvenhage’s comments followed the briefing reception on China’s zero-tariff treatment for African countries, hosted by Chinese Ambassador to South Africa Wu Peng in Pretoria on Thursday where he described the positive impact of the tariff move for South Africa.
The event, themed “Zero Tariffs, Zero Distance,” was jointly hosted with the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition and the South African Revenue Service.
“Zero tariffs mean that South African products can enter the Chinese market under the most favourable conditions. Zero distance means that businesses and consumers in the two countries will be brought closer together than ever before,” he said.
He said that China had implemented zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations from May 1.
“This makes China the first major economy in the world to unilaterally extend comprehensive zero-tariff treatment to all African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations. I remember that at midnight on 1 May, 24 tonnes of fresh apples from South Africa cleared through customs at China’s Shenzhen Bay Port. This became the first import to enter China under the new zero-tariff treatment,” he said.
Wu said since the implementation of zero-tariffs, China-South Africa economic and trade cooperation has continued to gain positive momentum.
“First, bilateral trade has grown significantly. According to SARS, trade between China and South Africa reached nearly 15 billion US dollars from May to August, an increase of nearly 24% year-on-year,” he said.
He added that South Africa's exports to China totalled US$9.47 billion, up 23% year-on-year while imports from China stood at US$9.47 billion, up 23% year-on-year.
“Maybe this is the first time South Africa’s exports to China outpace imports from China,” he said.
“With the Green Lane 2.0 announced by China, South African products such as wild aquatic products and dried chili have gained access to the Chinese market through the Regional Integrated Access. In September this year, China and South Africa signed a protocol for exporting South African cherries to China,” he said.
Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition Parks Tau said the briefing reception aimed to raise awareness of the tariff measure and provide a structured platform to address questions from South African businesses.
Tau said the zero-tariff treatment policy means China is implementing a unilateral preference scheme granting duty-free market access for 100% of the products, with the exception of 47 tariff lines subject to a tariff rate quota.
“This was announced by President Xi on 14 February 2026 in his congratulatory message to the AU Summit, and it is valid between 1 May 2026 – 30 April 2028. South African products that meet the rules of origin can enter the Chinese market without customs duties. From 1 June to 31 August, SARS issued 25 975 certificates of origin. Customs declarations rose by 199 percent year on year,” he said.
Tau said South Africa has already developed a Top 100 value-added product portfolio for the Chinese market.
“The portfolio cuts across agro-processing, beverages, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, machinery, medical equipment, fabricated metals, plastics and rubber, automotive products and other industrial capabilities,” he said.

articles.title: Brazil: Brazil's Runoff: Why a Bolsonaro Win Would Shake Europe's Trade Plans - Friedrich Naumann Foundation
articles.summary: Brazil: Brazil's Runoff: Why a Bolsonaro Win Would Shake Europe's Trade Plans  Friedrich Naumann Foundation
articles.full_text:
Why Brazil's Presidential Election Is Geopolitically Crucial for Europe
      
It is more than just a symbolic image. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro stands in the Oval Office of the White House. The 45-year-old wears a yellow-and-green-striped tie—the colors of Brazil—and stares intently into the camera. Seated at the desk in front of him, United States of America, President Donald Trump smiles broadly. The photo was taken on May 26 of this year. Although it was already clear by then that the eldest son of imprisoned former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro intended to run in the presidential election, he had not yet officially announced his candidacy. Nevertheless, he was certain of Trump’s support.
Just a few weeks earlier, the left-leaning incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had met with the USA president at the White House. The photos from that visit tell a different story. The two heads of state are seated across from each other in armchairs, Trump leaning forward and Lula gesturing wildly with his legs crossed. Lula, who is now campaigning for a fourth term, wanted to demonstrate strength on equal footing and project Brazil’s newfound foreign policy confidence to the world.
When Bolsonaro Jr. and Lula face off in the presidential runoff on October 25, it will not merely be a clash between two camps that have been at odds for nearly a decade. The USA is acting as a powerful player behind the scenes. Trump sees an opportunity to expand his strategic influence in Latin America.
In recent months, conservative politicians who favor closer ties with the major partner to the north have won every election in Latin America. So far, Brazil—the region’s most important economy—has been the exception. A victory for Bolsonaro Jr. in the runoff would therefore also be a victory for Trump. In the first round of the presidential election on October 4, the right-wing conservative politician led Lula by about three percentage points.
As expected, foreign policy issues are not at the center of the election campaign. Nevertheless, this election also involves a fundamental decision: How should Brazil position itself vis-à-vis the USA in the future?
A one-sided alignment with Washington would be a risk for Bolsonaro
The trade conflict that Trump instigated last year was sparked by Jair Bolsonaro’s sentencing to 27 years in prison for an attempted coup. Trump wielded the tariff stick and imposed additional duties on Brazilian exports. Behind this was an overt threat to Lula’s left-leaning government.
Most recently, in July, Trump imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods. Products such as beef and coffee were exempt. In doing so, the USA president spared powerful agricultural producers, who are key supporters of Bolsonaro Jr. Although Trump is not openly interfering in the Brazilian election campaign, he is nonetheless exerting influence through statements supporting Bolsonaro and his tariff policy.
While the USA. is aggressively pursuing its power politics, Europe remains in a wait-and-see mode. It is too uncertain how Bolsonaro Jr. will position himself on foreign policy as a potential new president. The only certainty is that ties with the USA are likely to grow closer. That would mark a break from the course of “active non-alignment” pursued by Lula.
In his campaign platform, Bolsonaro Jr. presents himself as moderate and avoids radical rhetoric. On foreign policy issues, however, he remains vague, and his statements are at times contradictory. This is evident in the EU-Mercosur agreement, the free trade initiative between Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay and the European Union.
Bolsonaro Jr. speaks of freeing Brazil “from the shackles” of the Mercosur agreement and relying more on bilateral treaties. He said he would “aggressively” seek new agreements. It remains unclear whether he is aiming for a complete withdrawal from the Mercosur agreement, a suspension, or renegotiations in certain areas, such as environmental protection requirements.
Bolsonaro Questions the EU-Mercosur Agreement
According to his own statements, one of his first actions will be to conclude a bilateral free trade agreement with the USA modeled after Argentina’s. This would grant the United States privileged market access. European suppliers would be left behind.
The stakes are high for the EU. After more than 25 rounds of negotiations, the agreement with the Mercosur countries was finally brought across the finish line this year—at least in terms of provisional implementation. Lula played a decisive role in this. It is his greatest foreign policy triumph.
However, even a slight weakening of the free trade agreement would be disastrous for Europe. This is because many EU countries, led by Germany, are struggling with sluggish growth and are counting on new markets in Brazil. At the same time, they are seeking to reduce their economic dependencies. Brazil possesses the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earth elements, has numerous offshore oil reserves that have not yet been developed, and intends to expand the mining of iron ore and critical raw materials.
Bolsonaro has also made an announcement regarding security policy that is likely to be noted with interest in Europe. He intends to join the “Shield of the Americas” security initiative, which was founded by Trump about eight months ago. The pact, which currently includes 19 Latin American countries, aims to combat cross-border drug trafficking and organized crime.
Lula Defends Multilateralism and Neutrality
As the USA assumes a leading role in the alliance, Trump’s influence in the region is growing. The two largest countries in Latin America, Brazil and Mexico, are currently led by center-left governments and have not yet joined the alliance. They fear that Washington could expand its claim to power in the region.
Bolsonaro Jr. also supports Trump’s decision to designate Brazil’s two largest criminal organizations, the PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital) and Comando Vermelho, as terrorist organizations. This marks another break with Lula’s foreign policy, as his administration had unsuccessfully argued against the move, citing Brazil’s sovereignty. Such a designation of criminal organizations gives the USA a stronger legal basis to crack down on the cartels—including through operations on Brazilian soil.
These examples show that the Brazilian presidential election has significance far beyond the country’s borders. A government under Lula would adhere to the traditional principles of Brazilian foreign policy: autonomy, multilateralism, and cooperation with various partners.
Bolsonaro, on the other hand, has announced a geopolitical reorientation. He would shift the focus toward the USA, while Europe would become less important. Efforts to strengthen partnerships and economic ties could thus suffer significant setbacks.
However, a foreign policy orientation that is one-sidedly aligned with the USA would also be risky for Bolsonaro Jr. Should he align himself closely with the White House, he could face resistance from within his own ranks. Political scientist Octavio Amorim Neto of the Getúlio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo anticipates conflicts with segments of the economic elite, nationalist forces within the armed forces, and major media conglomerates. He attributes this to economic interests and concerns that Brazil might sacrifice some of its autonomy if it were to form ties with Washington that are too close.
Uncertain Future for Brazil’s BRICS Membership
Bolsonaro Jr. has explicitly called into question not only the future of the Mercosur agreement but also Brazil’s BRICS membership. On his first day as president, he said in a podcast that he would examine whether Brazil should remain in an alliance that is ideologically driven and provokes the USA
Under the Lula administration, Brazil has advocated for a pragmatic and open approach to the alliance, which is anything but homogeneous. The BRICS should explicitly not be viewed as an anti-Western alliance, but rather as a means of pooling the political and economic interests of its member states. In 2025, Brazil hosted the BRICS summit. China, Russia, India, and Brazil are founding members of the alliance, which has since expanded.
In an increasingly multipolar world marked by growing tensions and conflicts, the BRICS group could continue to gain in importance. Brazil’s withdrawal would not only weaken the alliance; the South American country would also lose international influence and jeopardize its self-proclaimed role as a mediator between different centers of power.
Under Lula, Brazil has increasingly sought closer ties with Europe. Its support for the Mercosur agreement is one example of this. Further evidence is the decision not to join China’s “Belt and Road” initiative. In doing so, Brazil is attempting to limit its dependence on China and preserve its autonomy.
Brazil Remains a Key Geopolitical Player
With its renewed engagement in Latin America, the United States aims above all to curb China’s influence in the region—both economically and politically. But the groundwork has already been laid. China is by far Brazil’s largest trading partner, ahead of the USA Brazil is the world’s leading supplier of agricultural products to China, such as soybeans, beef, sugar, and corn. Brazilian farmers are thus in direct competition with American farmers and have a significant interest in securing their market access.
Should Bolsonaro Jr. win the election, he will have to face this economic reality. Unlike his father, he is promising a pragmatic approach to China in his campaign. Jair Bolsonaro once warned against a “sellout” of Brazil, but during his time in office, he expanded ties with China.
